label: June 2026 PYQ variants — Regression and linear models

items.stem: trace of the hat matrix H = X(X′X)⁻¹X′ with X of order n × k and full rank is:
items.explanation: The hat matrix H is a rank-k projection. The trace of a projection equals its rank, so tr(H)=k.

items.stem: If e = (I − H)y are the OLS residuals, then E(ee′) is:
items.explanation: With e=(I−H)u and Var(u)=σ²I, Var(e)=σ²(I−H)(I−H)′. Since I−H is symmetric and idempotent, this reduces to σ²(I−H).

items.stem: E(e′e) in the model y = Xβ + u with E(uu′) = σ²I is:
items.explanation: E(e′e)=tr{E(ee′)}=σ²tr(I−H). Since tr(H)=k, tr(I−H)=n−k, giving E(e′e)=σ²(n−k).

items.stem: Under normality, e′e/σ² follows:
items.explanation: Under normal errors, (I−H)u/σ is a normal projection onto a subspace of dimension n−k. Its squared length therefore follows χ² with n−k degrees of freedom.

items.stem: The product H(I − H) equals:
items.explanation: H is idempotent, so H²=H. Hence H(I−H)=H−H²=0.

items.stem: MX where M = I − X(X′X)⁻¹X′ equals:
items.explanation: M=I−X(X′X)⁻¹X′ annihilates every column of X. Therefore MX=0.

items.stem: The sum of the leverages Σhᵢᵢ in a regression with k parameters is:
items.explanation: The sum of the diagonal leverages is tr(H). Since H is a rank-k projection, tr(H)=k.

items.stem: The determinant of the idempotent matrix P = I − H (with 0 < k < n) is:
items.explanation: An idempotent projection I−H has k zero eigenvalues and n−k unit eigenvalues. Its determinant, the product of its eigenvalues, is zero.

items.stem: The rank of the projection matrix onto the column space of X (n × k, rank k) is:
items.explanation: The matrix X(X′X)⁻¹X′ projects onto the column space of X. Its rank equals the dimension of that space, namely k.

items.stem: When the errors have V(u) = σ²V with V ≠ I, the OLS estimator is:
items.explanation: When E(u|X)=0, OLS remains unbiased. With non-spherical error covariance it is generally not BLUE; GLS is the efficient linear unbiased estimator under the specified covariance structure.

items.stem: The unbiased estimator of σ² in a model with n observations and k parameters is:
items.explanation: Under the classical linear model, E(e′e)=σ²(n−k). Dividing the residual sum of squares by its residual degrees of freedom gives the unbiased estimator σ̂²=e′e/(n−k).

items.stem: For y₁ = β₁ + β₂ + u₁, y₂ = β₁ − β₂ + u₂ with equal variances, the BLUE of β₂ is:
items.explanation: The design matrix has rows (1,1) and (1,−1), so X′X=2I. Thus β̂₂ is the second component of (X′X)⁻¹X′y, equal to (y₁−y₂)/2.

items.stem: In the Gauss–Markov set-up, “best” means:
options: minimum variance among linear unbiased estimators
items.explanation: In the Gauss–Markov theorem, 'best' means having the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators of the same estimable function.

items.stem: With n = 50, k = 5 and R² = 0.55, the adjusted R² is:
items.explanation: Adjusted R²=1−(1−R²)(n−1)/(n−k). Substitution gives 1−0.45×49/45=0.51.

items.stem: The degrees of freedom of the overall F statistic in a model with n observations and k parameters are:
items.explanation: The overall regression F statistic compares regression mean square with residual mean square. Their degrees of freedom are k−1 and n−k, respectively.

items.stem: In simple linear regression, the relation between the overall F and the t-statistic for the slope is:
items.explanation: With one slope restriction, the overall F test and the two-sided t test for the slope are equivalent. The relationship is F=t².

items.stem: As R² approaches 1, the F-statistic:
items.explanation: F=[R²/(k−1)]/[(1−R²)/(n−k)]. As R²→1, the denominator tends to zero while the numerator remains positive, so F→∞.

items.stem: Adding an irrelevant regressor to a model will:
options: leave R² unchanged or increase it
items.explanation: Adding a regressor enlarges the set of possible fitted values; the old fit remains available by setting the new coefficient to zero. RSS cannot increase, so R² cannot decrease.

items.stem: Adjusted R² can be:
items.explanation: Adjusted R² subtracts a degrees-of-freedom penalty from the ordinary fit measure. If the fit is weak relative to the number of parameters, the adjusted value can be negative.

items.stem: An ANOVA table gives RegSS = 66870 with 3 df and RSS = 5344 with 16 df. The F-ratio is:
In multiple regression, R² equals:
items.explanation: With an intercept, TSS=RegSS+RSS. Therefore R²=RegSS/TSS=1−RSS/TSS.

items.stem: A high R² together with individually insignificant t-statistics suggests:
items.explanation: Multicollinearity makes coefficient estimates imprecise by inflating their standard errors. The model can still have high overall explanatory power and a significant joint F test.

items.stem: The unbiased estimator of σ² in a model with k parameters is:
items.explanation: For k estimated parameters, E(RSS)=σ²(n−k). Hence RSS/(n−k) is unbiased for σ².

items.stem: In the model y = Xβ + u with E(u) = 0 and V(u) = σ²I, the OLS estimator is BLUE. This requires:
options: no distributional assumption beyond the first two moments
items.explanation: The Gauss–Markov theorem requires a correctly specified linear conditional mean, zero conditional error mean, spherical error covariance and full column rank. Normality is not required for BLUE.

items.stem: The variance–covariance matrix of the OLS estimator is:
items.explanation: Using β̂=(X′X)⁻¹X′y and Var(u|X)=σ²I gives Var(β̂|X)=σ²(X′X)⁻¹.

items.stem: If y₁ = β + u₁, y₂ = 2β + u₂ with equal variances, the BLUE of β is:
items.explanation: For X=(1,2)′, X′X=1²+2²=5 and X′y=y₁+2y₂. Thus β̂=(y₁+2y₂)/5.

items.stem: In question 3, the variance of the BLUE is:
items.explanation: The variance of the estimator in the preceding design is σ²(X′X)⁻¹=σ²/5.

items.stem: If X′X is diagonal, the least squares estimators of the parameters are:
items.explanation: If X′X is diagonal, its inverse is diagonal. Since Var(β̂|X)=σ²(X′X)⁻¹, the coefficient estimators have zero pairwise covariances.

items.stem: A linear parametric function ℓ′β is estimable if:
options: ℓ′ lies in the row space of X
items.explanation: A linear function ℓ′β is estimable exactly when ℓ lies in the row space of X, equivalently when ℓ′=a′X for some vector a.

items.stem: Which of the following DOES cause bias in the OLS estimator?
options: omission of a relevant variable correlated with an included regressor
items.explanation: Omitting a relevant variable correlated with an included regressor makes the included regressor correlated with the composite error, creating omitted-variable bias.

items.stem: With E(u|X)=0, under heteroscedasticity OLS is:
items.explanation: Under E(u|X)=0, heteroscedasticity alone does not bias OLS. It generally makes OLS inefficient relative to GLS and invalidates conventional homoscedastic standard errors.

items.stem: Principal component regression addresses multicollinearity by:
options: using orthogonal linear combinations of the regressors
items.explanation: Principal component regression replaces correlated predictors with orthogonal principal-component scores and can retain selected components to reduce multicollinearity.

items.stem: Multicollinearity primarily damages:
items.explanation: Multicollinearity inflates standard errors and makes separate coefficient effects hard to interpret. It need not damage overall fit or prediction within the observed data range.

items.stem: Adding an extra regressor to a linear model causes R² to:
items.explanation: Adding a regressor cannot increase the residual sum of squares in a nested least-squares model. With total sum of squares fixed, R² can only increase or stay the same.

items.stem: Adjusted R² differs from R² in that it:
items.explanation: Adjusted R² modifies ordinary R² by penalising the number of estimated parameters, so an added regressor must improve fit enough to offset the degrees-of-freedom penalty.

items.stem: The residual sum of squares of a model with more parameters, compared with a nested submodel, is:
items.explanation: The larger nested model contains all fits available to the smaller model. Minimising over a larger parameter set cannot produce a larger residual sum of squares.

items.stem: Adjusted R² can decrease when a regressor is added because:
options: the df penalty outweighs the fall in RSS
items.explanation: Adjusted R² can fall when the improvement in RSS is too small to compensate for the loss of residual degrees of freedom caused by adding a parameter.

items.stem: When q = 1, the partial F-statistic equals:
items.explanation: For one restriction, the partial F statistic has one numerator degree of freedom and equals the square of the corresponding t statistic.

items.stem: Fitting a polynomial of degree n − 1 through n points gives RSS equal to:
items.explanation: A polynomial of degree n−1 can interpolate n observations at distinct x values exactly. Every fitted residual is zero, so RSS=0.

items.stem: Between AIC and BIC, the criterion that penalises extra parameters more heavily for large n is:
items.explanation: AIC uses a penalty of 2k, whereas BIC uses k log(n). For n>e², log(n)>2, so BIC penalises additional parameters more heavily.

items.stem: If the estimated coefficient of the added term is exactly zero, then A and B satisfy:
items.explanation: If the added coefficient is estimated as zero, the larger model gives the same fitted values as the restricted model. Their residual sums of squares are equal.

items.stem: Mallows’ Cₚ is used for:
items.explanation: Mallows' Cₚ is a model-selection criterion used to compare subsets of predictors, balancing residual fit against model complexity.

items.stem: The variance inflation factor for regressor j is:
items.explanation: For regressor j, VIFⱼ=1/(1−Rⱼ²), where Rⱼ² comes from regressing that predictor on all the other predictors.

items.stem: A VIF exceeding which value is commonly taken as a warning?
items.explanation: A VIF above 10 is a commonly used warning threshold for potentially serious multicollinearity. It is a heuristic, not a universal cutoff.

items.stem: The classic symptom of multicollinearity is:
options: low R² with significant t values
high R² with insignificant t values
items.explanation: When regressors are highly correlated, the model may explain y well overall while individual coefficient standard errors are large. This produces high R² but insignificant individual t tests.

items.stem: Ridge regression estimates are:
items.explanation: Ridge regression adds a penalty to the least-squares objective. This introduces some bias but can substantially reduce coefficient variance and improve stability.

items.stem: If H is a rank-k orthogonal projection matrix of order n, then the trace of I−H is:
items.explanation: An idempotent projection has trace equal to its rank. Since rank(H)=k, trace(I−H)=n−trace(H)=n−k.

items.stem: In two nested least-squares models, the larger model adds one regressor. The residual sum of squares can remain unchanged precisely when:
options: The added coefficient is estimated as zero
items.explanation: The restricted model is contained in the larger model. If the fitted coefficient of the added regressor is zero, the larger model reproduces the restricted fit and both residual sums of squares are equal.

items.stem: Assume the regression model is correctly specified and errors are exogenous. Near multicollinearity by itself does not make the OLS coefficient estimator:
items.explanation: Near multicollinearity makes coefficient estimates imprecise and unstable, inflating variances and standard errors. Under the stated exogeneity assumptions, it does not by itself introduce bias.
